from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image,ImageOps,ImageDraw
p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
for name,pages in [('intro',[1,2,3,4]),('method',[6,7,16,17]),('results',[18,19,20,21]),('qualitative',[22,23])]:
    thumbs=[]
    for n in pages:
        im=Image.open(p/f'page-{n:02d}.png').convert('RGB')
        im.thumbnail((702,910))
        panel=Image.new('RGB',(712,940),'white')
        panel.paste(im,((712-im.width)//2,25))
        ImageDraw.Draw(panel).text((8,5),f'PAGE {n}',fill='black')
        thumbs.append(panel)
    contact=Image.new('RGB',(712*2,940*((len(thumbs)+1)//2)), '#aaaaaa')
    for k,im in enumerate(thumbs):contact.paste(im,(712*(k%2),940*(k//2)))
    contact.save(p/f'{name}-contact.png')
print('Created contact sheets for remaining content pages.')
PY"

strengths: The conditional summary graph is a useful contribution. Under the assumption that each variable’s outgoing effects depend on its own state, K graphs compactly represent up to K^N joint state configurations. Combining this representation with amortized graph inference is a well-motivated extension of ACD.

The synthetic experiments demonstrate substantial gains in several settings. For hidden-state, two-edge linear data, Table 2 reports 97.08% summary-graph accuracy versus 60.45% for ACD, alongside 98.08% conditional-summary-graph accuracy. The observed-state experiments and fixed-decoder ablations provide additional evidence that the approach can recover the intended interactions.

The evaluation includes linear systems, interacting particles, data-efficiency tests, transfer across system sizes, and NBA forecasting. The NBA results support practical predictive utility, while the graph illustrations and implementation appendices help explain the method. The paper also explicitly acknowledges the absence of hidden-state identifiability and estimator-consistency guarantees.
weaknesses: The headline identifiability result needs a more complete statement and proof. Theorem 1 omits the nonconstant-mechanism assumption used in Lemma 2. Appendix A.3 then infers dependence conditional on all other lagged variables from minimality conditional on the other parents; this requires additional support/intersection arguments. The conditions under which conditioning on the observed state sequence preserves independent noise should also be explicit, particularly for endogenous states. These gaps affect the claimed theoretical guarantee.

The comparisons do not sufficiently establish the advantage over methods designed for changing graph structures. Regime-PCMCI, identified as closely related in Table 1, is not evaluated. ACD assumes a stationary graph, while the paper itself explains that TdCM, CD-NOD, and SAEM are poorly suited to the simulated abrupt changes. Furthermore, SDCI receives 50,000 training sequences whereas the non-amortized methods fit individual sequences. These comparisons demonstrate utility in the chosen setting but do not isolate the benefit of the proposed representation from switching capability and shared-data training.

The evidence for hidden-state discovery is narrower than the introduction suggests. Appendix F.2 explicitly reports failure to recover accurate structures for hidden states in scenario class 3 and instead supplies state information. Successful hidden-state experiments primarily use simple deterministic functions of current observations and known state counts; the linear data are additionally filtered for balanced state visitation. The claims should distinguish these successes from the unresolved problem of recovering history-dependent hidden states.

The graph metrics leave an important part of the central claim insufficiently tested. Figure 5 evaluates the union summary graph rather than the state-dependent structure, so good performance need not imply correct switching behavior. Union graphs can also have substantial class imbalance: two independent graphs with 50% edge probability produce a union with 75% edge probability. Reporting graph density, majority baselines, conditional or time-resolved precision/recall, and quantitative hidden-state recovery would make the nonlinear results much more convincing.

NBA forecasting improvements do not establish causal correctness or show that causal discovery causes the predictive gains. There is no causal ground truth, and VRNN differs substantially in architecture and inductive bias. A comparable non-causal graph predictor or state-conditioned model is needed to isolate the contribution of inferred causal structure. The learned court partitions provide plausible descriptive interpretations, but do not independently validate causal relationships.

Several reporting gaps impede reproduction and assessment of reliability. The number of independent training runs and meaning of error bars are unspecified; Appendix C.2 introduces an undefined lambda; the graph prior and state-network architecture are not fully specified. The NBA split protocol and availability of ball features during future rollout also need clarification. These omissions matter for interpreting both uncertainty and forecasting difficulty.
